title: Japan Hiked Visa Fees Fivefold — but Indians Still Pay ₹500
excerpt: Tokyo's first visa price revision in 48 years spares Indian passport holders, making Japan one of the cheapest long-haul visas for the diaspora even as costs soar for everyone else.
body:
Japan just raised its visa fees for the first time since 1978. The increase is dramatic — a fivefold jump that took effect on July 1, 2026 — and it touches nearly every nationality that needs a visa to enter the country. But Indian passport holders are exempt. They will continue paying ₹500 for both single-entry and multiple-entry tourist visas, making Japan arguably the cheapest long-haul visa available to Indian travellers anywhere in the world.

The numbers tell the story. A single-entry Japanese visa now costs JPY 15,000 (roughly ₹8,760) for most foreign nationals, up from JPY 3,000. A multiple-entry visa has jumped from JPY 6,000 to JPY 30,000 (about ₹17,520). For Indians, the price hasn't moved: ₹500, regardless of visa type. Add the VFS Global service charge of ₹800, and the total out-of-pocket for an Indian applicant comes to ₹1,300 — less than the price of a decent sushi dinner in Mumbai.

## Why India got a pass

Japanese authorities haven't publicly explained the exemption, but it almost certainly traces to bilateral visa fee arrangements between the two countries. India and Japan have steadily deepened diplomatic and economic ties over the past decade, and visa policy has been one of the quieter instruments of that relationship. The exemption predates this revision and has simply been carried forward.

The application process for Indians is also unchanged. No prior appointment is needed. Payments are accepted in rupees — cash, card, or UPI — and processing takes roughly six working days. Japanese consulates have warned, though, that peak-season volumes could stretch that timeline.

## What's behind the hike

The revision is part of a broader overhaul of Japan's immigration fee structure. The previous rates had remained frozen for nearly half a century, surviving decades of inflation, currency shifts, and a complete transformation in how immigration systems operate. Japan's foreign resident population recently crossed four million for the first time, and the government says the additional revenue will support consular administration, expand Japanese-language programmes for residents, and strengthen enforcement against visa overstays.

Japan's parliament cleared the enabling legislation earlier this year, with the Lower House passing the bill in April and the Upper House in May. Officials have framed the new pricing as bringing Japan's visa charges closer to G7 norms — a reasonable argument, given that a US B1/B2 visa costs $185 and a Schengen visa runs €80.

Further changes are expected. Residency-related fees — including permanent residency applications, status changes, and stay extensions — have also been raised, with more revisions slated through March 2027.

## What NRIs should know

For Indian Americans planning a Japan trip, the takeaway is straightforward: book with confidence. Japan remains one of the few major tourist destinations where Indian passport holders face almost no visa cost barrier. The ₹500 fee is a fraction of what travellers pay for visas to Australia (AUD 190), the UK (£115), or even Canada (CAD 100).

Japan has also become significantly more accessible from India in recent years. Air India operates nonstop Mumbai–Tokyo Haneda flights (launched just weeks ago), and IndiGo has been expanding its Asian network aggressively. Multiple Gulf carriers offer competitive one-stop options from US cities through Dubai or Doha.

The practical advice: apply early if you're travelling during cherry blossom season (late March–April) or autumn foliage (October–November), when processing times tend to stretch. And remember that the visa exemption covers tourism — work visas, student visas, and long-term residency follow different rules and different fee schedules.

At a time when visa costs are rising almost everywhere, Japan's decision to hold the line for Indian travellers is a quiet but meaningful gesture. For the roughly five million Indian Americans who hold Indian passports, it makes Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka some of the most affordable international destinations to access on paper — even if the flight and the omakase dinner are another story entirely.
